extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, government administrators, political scientists, and reformers interested in designing or evaluating governmental/industrial intelligence and research bureaus
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organising, staffing, funding, and operating intelligence/research bureaus in government and industry so they reliably inform decision‑makers without becoming partisan or ossified. Emphasises institutional safeguards, measurement standards, coordination, and links with universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert role: prepare facts for decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert should 'prepare the facts for the men of action' so that the disinterested expert 'first finds and formulates the facts for the man of action, and later makes what wisdom he can out of comparison between the decision... and the facts he organized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid an ex post facto relationship where the social scientist merely rationalizes decisions after they are made; experts should supply usable facts in time to shape decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality / non-advocacy of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts must separate themselves from those who make decisions and avoid having a 'policy' or expressing preference about what decision should be made (e.g., 'the very last thing ... will tolerate ... is the suspicion that they have a "policy."').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experts begin to care too much about outcomes they 'see what they wish to see' and cease to represent unseen interests faithfully; remain neutral in expert role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigation and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff which executes should be distinct from the staff which investigates: 'The two should be parallel but quite distinct bodies of men, recruited differently, paid if possible from separate funds, responsible to different heads.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional separation reduces the tendency of investigators to absorb decision functions and prevents investigators becoming subordinate to managers whose performance they must examine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence rests on funds, tenure, and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence of intelligence bureaus 'will turn mainly on three points on funds, tenure, and access to the facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional protections in all three dimensions to prevent a Congress or departmental official from making the bureau its creature by withholding money, dismissing staff, or closing files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure and protected funding
rubrics_metrics.description: No agency of research can be really free if it depends on annual doles; funding should be insulated (examples: federal charter creating a trust fund, sliding scale tied to department appropriation) so 'the appropriation should be put beyond accident.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanisms (trust funds, sliding scales, protected appropriations) that make attacks on the bureau's existence require open repeal rather than surreptitious undermining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure protections for investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure should be for life with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, sabbatical years for study/training, and dismissal only after a trial by professional colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide dignity and security so investigators have intellectual freedom and are not immediately concerned with practical decision pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory access to materials and investigatory powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureau should have 'the right to examine all papers, and to question any official or any outsider' and this access 'should be established in the organic act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant the right to propose accounting methods and, if rejected or violated, the ability to appeal under charter to Congress; ensure continuous investigation differs from sensational or spasmodic inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role as the Congressional oversight link
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intelligence bureau should be 'the connecting link between Congress and the Department' and act as 'the Congressional eye on the execution of its policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making departmental operation permanently visible the bureau can reduce the impulse for minute, distrustful legislation and serve as departmental answer to Congressional criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and index numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus should 'adopt, wherever possible, standards of measurement that were comparable' and 'if you can contrive the right index numbers ... you can set up a competition' to promote desired aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create quantitative measures (broadly defined 'index numbers') to compare schools, factories, departments, etc.; examples cited include Leonard P. Ayres' index for state school systems and quota applications like Liberty Loan campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination, data exchange, and central clearing house
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish central clearing houses and exchange records so departments can draw on information already obtained elsewhere (e.g., State Department calling on a diplomatic intelligence bureau that draws from the central clearing house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central agency becomes a focus of extraordinary information and helps assemble facts in forms suited to specific problems; beware perverted uses (trade association abuses noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary over-centralization; use comparable measures to enable competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Different departments need not do the same work through a single agency if they 'use the same measure for the same things' so units can be treated as competitors without cumbersome over-centralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select goals and rules of competition carefully; comparable measures let competition serve higher aims rather than money/power/popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and training linked with universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff may be recruited from college graduates, with a circulation of temporary and specialist appointments from universities and exchange lecturers, creating a 'national university' connection to training and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use turnover and academic links to keep methods current and to supply trained personnel; part of research can be done by students under consultation with the national agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on practical utility for men of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Primarily the intelligence bureau is 'an instrument of the man of action, of the representative charged with decision, of the worker at his work'—not to burden every citizen with expert opinion on all questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reports to assist administrators and decision-makers; public dissemination and press-checking are secondary benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make invisible environments visible and usable
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence work should 'make the machine visible' and represent 'unseen factors' (e.g., comparative statistics of infant mortality made babies visible leading to policy changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making social processes visible you enable self-criticism, reduce trial and error, and confront material forces with a changed environment that can reshape decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional/federated organisation to match effective environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the principle to states, cities, and counties through federations of bureaus and regional coordination because 'legal frontiers often do not coincide with the effective environments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate accounting systems and information across jurisdictions (e.g., metropolitan problems like health and transportation) to reconcile autonomy with cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against bureaucratic decay via circulation and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges the risk that intelligence bureaus may become 'a dead weight'—attractive to 'men in search of soft jobs' and produce 'red tape, mountains of papers'—so mitigate by 'circulation of men, a circulation of data and of criticism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote turnover, data sharing, academic exchange, and public visibility to reduce dry rot and make the bureau simplify rather than complicate administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intelligence to reduce minute legislation and enable better federalism
rubrics_metrics.description: By making departmental operations permanently visible, intelligence bureaus may 'cease to feel the need of that minute legislation born of distrust' and help federalism function 'more and more by consent, less and less by coercion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intelligence as a substitute for over-prescriptive lawmaking; provide shared facts and common measures to base cooperative federal arrangements.
